title: The Redzone/Wrestle Trial of Steve Lee
summary: Chapter 14 opens with a damaged Mangchi performance and then stages two intertwined trials: a literal series of wrestling bouts and a continuing test of whether Steve Lee keeps his job with David Choe. Steve reads a self-authored contract covering punctuality, Mangchi/Igloo Hong work, health, preparation and creative contribution. David makes the next wrestling result an explicit job-retention condition, outweighs Steve by roughly seventy pounds, loses the declared bout, concedes that Steve won fairly, and later proposes another employment rematch. The record therefore keeps together Steve's authorship and stated desire for the job, David's employer/benefactor power, the physical-risk warnings, direct ‘don't touch me’ statements, back/neck injuries, disputed rules and video dependence. The episode then uses Steve's ‘red zone’ as a theory about anger around money and sex. A Hawaii catfish story supplies evidence of a genuine safety concern—requests for legal name and home address—but never proves the private woman was fake or committing fraud. David accesses Steve's phone without permission and sends an abusive message in his voice; Steve and the room call that action wrong. The comedy-material dispute similarly preserves every boundary: Steve, Bobby Lee and Khalyla warn David not to copy Bobby's act or sabotage a paid show, and Khalyla names the private aftermath she would absorb. David ultimately does not perform the copied act. The Hawaii shows become an account of improvisation, audience warm-up, friendship and opportunity, with several career claims later exposed as a prank. Daniel Dae Kim's attendance and praise are reported conversations; a Netflix representative, hot-Asian list and some praise were explicitly invented to manipulate Bobby's mood. The editorial layer never upgrades the residual production-company interest into a completed project. A first-class/window-seat argument leads to Khalyla's direct disclosure of bipolar disorder, depression and past suicidal intent. Those statements remain a mental-health signal, not entertainment diagnosis. The 2011 tears study did find reduced male testosterone and arousal after men sniffed women's emotional tears in a controlled experiment, but it does not establish the episode's universal claim that crying makes male partners annoyed. An injured-bird story contains ableist language, intentional prey attraction, a cat attack, proposed neck-snapping, attempted rescue and death; every event remains, while the public layer avoids making animal harm a challenge or method. Another story reports genital contact while David slept and its later reuse as stage material. Prior friendship, a joke or ‘no homo’ does not create consent to contact or publication. The episode repeatedly pressures Steve to identify and describe a private sexual partner after he asks to change subjects, says he dislikes the questions and says stop. Those objections control over earlier disclosures and a public-interview-training rationale. Pregnancy, birth-control honesty and abortion are speculative. CDC guidance confirms that withdrawal does not protect against STIs and has materially higher typical-use failure than many contraceptive methods; hormonal contraception also does not protect against STIs. The later married-couple discussion includes another direct request to keep sex private, followed immediately by more detail. The closing trivia/smell sequence includes repeated pressure, direct no statements and an apparent physical act that requires video. The episode ends with rough ‘Gook Boy’ lyrics: the slur, violence and alienation remain in the source layer, but uncertain lyrics are not silently polished into quotations. Across all topics, private partners, contact details, intimate images, reproductive plans, assistants, finances and nonpublic venue/person trails stay out of neutral discovery. Episode-level cast context may identify public people, but no line-level speaker names publish because no held-out acoustic turns pass validation.

connections.note: Creative-opportunity discipline returns, but Chapter 14 shows how readiness advice changes when an employer attaches work to physical compliance.
The self-contract and album plug connect fitness, rehearsal, promotion and live performance to the band's operational demands.
The episode documents the public-stage-name spelling, music/comedy development and the recurring tension between privacy, employment and performance.
The restaurant job functions as Steve's lower-paid fallback and a comparison point for employer expectations.
Their Hawaii travel, comedy work and relationship become both evidence and material; Khalyla repeatedly names downstream costs and privacy boundaries.
Maui and Honolulu are distinct comedy shows; participants disagree about video capture, so the source ledger should not imply footage exists until recovered.

connections.to: Daniel Dae Kim and Grace Park
connections.note: Their reported attendance anchors the Honolulu show, while later production and praise claims must remain attributed conversations.
Bobby's official cast presence is real; the episode's grievance concerns promotional billing and status, not whether he appeared.
A booking-coordinator change triggers the career-anchor discussion; allegations about a former employee remain attributed and unverified.
The farewell appearance becomes a comparison point for perceived career heat and peer advancement.

connections.to: The Pig and the Lady / Hawaii food
connections.note: The restaurant story mixes praise with an acute gastrointestinal episode; timing does not establish a foodborne cause.
Profile help and public exposure produce more matches, but do not waive a later partner's identity or intimate privacy.
The 2011 laboratory result is narrower than the room's universal relationship theory and should be linked as correction, not endorsement.
The pregnancy/STI discussion needs a corrective source because withdrawal and reported pill use are treated too casually.
Normal commercial pressurization and high-altitude hypoxia guidance do not support the claimed automatic sleep response when the cabin door closes.
The bird story combines intentional prey attraction, injury, attempted rescue, family memory and death rather than fitting a single comedy beat.
Reported genital contact during sleep remains a consent issue even when retold as friendship or stage material.
The rejected plan to copy a headliner's act parallels the corpus rule that transformation and commentary do not erase attribution or permission.
The closing song preserves the slur and difficult ideas while uncertain performed words remain non-quotation-grade.

source_notes: The machine cleaner records 182 edits: 152 empty artifacts and thirty degenerate-run removals. It reduces 3,122 raw segments to 2,953 clean segments.

The apparent word increase from 23,342 raw to 23,356 clean is exact and non-substantive: 51 hallucinated or degenerate words are removed and thirteen five-word `[indistinct audio - not transcribable]` markers add 65 descriptive tokens, a net increase of fourteen without invented dialogue.

The separate human fixture contains 389 sorted correction/context decisions spanning 1–7,844 seconds. It is the substantive transcript-improvement layer; the cleaner alone is not accepted as a human audit.
The opening performance and final `Gook Boy` performance contain unstable ASR. Song ideas and the slur remain visible, but uncertain words are labelled rather than silently reconstructed.

The official *Awesomes* site identifies the program as a Hulu original and displays Bobby Lee among the cast. It supports cast presence, not the episode's claims about promotional-star billing or relative fame: https://theawesomes.com/

PubMed's record for Gelstein et al., *Human tears contain a chemosignal* (Science, 2011; PMID 21212322) reports reduced male-rated sexual appeal, self-rated arousal, physiological arousal and testosterone after sniffing women's negative-emotion tears. The experiment does not establish that crying universally annoys male partners or explains every relationship response: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21212322/

FAA guidance says significant altitude-hypoxia effects generally do not occur in a normal healthy pilot below 12,000 feet and notes that transport cabins are normally pressurized below 8,000 feet. It does not support a universal cabin-door sleep reflex: https://www.faa.gov/Air_traffic/publications/atpubs/aim_html/chap8_section_1.html

CDC's contraception overview says most contraceptive methods do not protect against STIs and that condoms can help protect against HIV and other STIs: https://www.cdc.gov/contraception/about/index.html

CDC's withdrawal guidance says withdrawal does not protect against STIs, including HIV. Historical CDC effectiveness tables list a 22% first-year typical-use pregnancy rate and 4% perfect-use rate; therefore ‘just pull out’ is not adequate general safety advice: https://www.cdc.gov/contraception/hcp/usmec/coitus-interruptus-withdrawal.html and https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr6304a5.htm

The transcript itself explicitly reveals that the Netflix guest, hot-Asian list and several related praise statements were fabricated. Any residual claim that an agent heard from Daniel Dae Kim's production company remains unverified and must not be represented as a commission, special or completed deal.
Participants disagree about whether the Honolulu show was videotaped. Full-video recovery remains required before visual performance or wrestling assertions can be treated as verified.

Daniel Dae Kim/Grace Park attendance, The Pig and the Lady dinner, Migrant meal, Comedy Store scheduling, Chelsea finale, Hawaii promoter, bookstore acquaintance and other career accounts are speaker-reported unless an independent source is attached later.

Episode-level cast context strongly suggests David Choe, Steve Lee, Bobby Lee, Khalyla, Asa Akira, Bill Poon, Critter Fleming and recurring production voices. That context is not acoustic line-level validation.

Daniel Dae Kim, Grace Park, Robin Williams, Allen Ginsberg, Seth Meyers, Ike Barinholtz, Rachel Dratch, Kenan Thompson, Taran Killam, Marc Maron, Bill Burr, Chelsea Handler, Quentin Tarantino and other public figures may be indexed only where actually discussed. No line-level named dialogue publishes because the episode has zero accepted held-out identity windows and zero acoustically validated turns.
